keyTakeaways: A theatre script carries meaning through formatting and document regions as well as words.
Indentation, styles, punctuation, and capitalisation are evidence to combine—not universal classification rules.
Preserving the original Word .docx structure can produce a clearer, reviewable surtitle cue draft than flattening the script to plain text.
Human review and rehearsal remain responsible for cue boundaries, speaker attribution, translation, presentation, and timing.

faq.question: Why does script formatting matter for theatre surtitles?
faq.answer: Formatting can reveal speaker relationships, dialogue blocks, directions, headings, and document regions that the words alone do not identify.

faq.question: Are italics or colons reliable enough on their own?
faq.answer: No. Both can be strong signals, but their meaning depends on neighbouring text and patterns elsewhere in the document.

faq.question: What script format does SurtitleLive currently analyse?
faq.answer: The supported script-analysis input is an original Word .docx file. PDF and other non-DOCX formats are outside the current analysis workflow.

faq.question: Does layout-aware parsing replace human review?
faq.answer: No. It prepares an editable draft; the production team still checks the content and rehearses how it will be delivered.

glossary.definition: A part of a script, such as front matter, the performable body, or an appendix, whose content follows a distinct purpose or pattern.
Formatting evidence such as indentation, alignment, spacing, style, or punctuation that may help identify a script element.
The structured document format underlying Word .docx files, which can preserve paragraph and text formatting.
A document-layout unit equal to one twentieth of a point.
An editable sequence prepared from a script for human review, correction, translation, and rehearsal before live delivery.
